title: Feature Importance
abstract:
How much does each feature contribute to the prediction of the target? This
document covers the three techniques from the notes — SHAP, decision-tree
impurity reduction, and random-forest importance — explains impurity precisely,
adds the permutation method that fixes impurity importance's well-documented
biases, works through the two traps (high-cardinality features and correlated
features), and shows how importance functions as a feature-selection technique.

blocks.t: What It Is
From the notes

items: Means to calculate the importance of every feature / column.
It is a feature selection technique.
We can keep important features and remove unnecessary ones.

Basically the feature importance score tells us how much each
 feature contributes to the prediction of the target.

blocks.t: From the notes: the definition of impurity
Impurity $=$ how mixed / confused the data is in a node.

items: Node has all the same class: impurity $=0$.
Node has different classes mixed: impurity $>0$.

blocks.t:
This is the entropy/Gini of Topic 55, and it is the quantity all tree-based
importance measures are built from.
The Techniques
From the notes

items:
Measures the exact contribution of each feature. If I
 remove one feature, how much the prediction changes tells the importance.

The feature that reduces the impurity most is the
 most important.

How important is one feature to one or more trees
 — not just based on one tree. How much overall impurity it reduces.

blocks.t: Impurity-based importance, precisely

For a single tree, the importance of feature $j$ is the total weighted impurity
decrease produced by every node that split on it:

\text{Imp}(j)=\sum_{\text{nodes } t \text{ splitting on } j}
 \frac{n_t}{n}\left[I(t)-\frac{n_L}{n_t}I(t_L)-\frac{n_R}{n_t}I(t_R)\right],

normalised to sum to 1. The bracket is exactly the information gain of Topic 55,
and the $n_t/n$ factor weights a node by how much data passes through it — so a
split near the root counts for far more than one deep in a branch.

For a random forest, average this over all trees. That averaging is what
the notes mean by "how important is one feature to one or more trees, not
just based on one tree", and it is what makes forest importance far more stable
than a single tree's: one tree's greedy choices are arbitrary (Topic 54), but 300
trees' averaged choices are not.

blocks.cap:
Seven features — three carrying real signal, three pure noise, and a
 unique row ID. Impurity-based importance gives row_id a substantial
 score; permutation importance, measured on held-out data, correctly gives it
 none.

blocks.t: The Two Traps
Trap 1 — the cardinality bias

Impurity importance is computed on the training data, so a feature with
many distinct values can always find a split that separates the training rows a
little further — purely by chance. A unique ID column can therefore receive a
large importance while having zero predictive value, exactly as it received
maximum information gain in Topic 55.

The bias favours: continuous features over discrete ones, high-cardinality
categoricals over binary ones, and any feature with many possible split points.
Never compare impurity importances across features of very different
cardinality.
Trap 2 — correlated features split the credit

If two features carry the same information, each tree picks one arbitrarily, so
the importance is divided between them. Both then look moderately important, and
a naive selection rule that drops everything below a threshold may drop
both.

blocks.cap:
Adding a near-duplicate of signal_1 roughly halves its
 importance. Neither copy looks important alone, although together they remain
 the strongest predictor.

blocks.t: Permutation Importance — the Fix
The method

items: Score the fitted model on a held-out set: $s$.

Randomly shuffle column $j$ — destroying its relationship with $y$ while
 preserving its marginal distribution — and re-score: $s_j$.
Importance of $j$ is $s-s_j$. Repeat and average.

blocks.t:
This is the notes' SHAP intuition — if I remove one feature, how much the
prediction changes tells the importance — made computable. It is
model-agnostic, it is measured on data the model never saw, and it is
therefore immune to the cardinality bias: shuffling a useless ID column changes
nothing.
What SHAP adds

SHAP assigns each feature its Shapley value — from cooperative game
theory, the unique attribution satisfying efficiency, symmetry and additivity.
Its distinguishing property is that it is computed per prediction, so it
answers "why was this loan declined?" rather than only "which features
matter overall". Averaging the absolute values across rows recovers a global
importance. TreeSHAP computes it exactly for tree ensembles in polynomial
time, which is why SHAP is standard practice with XGBoost and LightGBM.
Permutation importance also struggles with correlated features

Shuffling one of two duplicated features leaves the model able to recover the
information from the other, so both appear unimportant. It also evaluates
the model on impossible feature combinations. Remedies: permute correlated
features as a group, or use conditional permutation. No importance measure
handles correlation perfectly — the question "which of two identical features
matters?" has no answer.
Using It for Feature Selection

blocks.cap:
Rank features by importance, then add them one at a time and
 cross-validate. Accuracy plateaus once the genuinely informative features are
 in — the rest can be removed.

blocks.t: The correct procedure

The notes' "we can keep important features and remove unnecessary ones"
needs one refinement: validate the selection. Ranking by importance and
cutting at an arbitrary threshold is guesswork. Instead, rank, then sweep the
number kept and cross-validate, and take the smallest set whose score is
statistically indistinguishable from the best. SelectFromModel and
RFECV automate this.

And do the selection inside the cross-validation loop — selecting on
the full dataset and then cross-validating is the leakage of Topic 17, and it
produces impressive scores on pure noise.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel, RFECV
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
X = np.c_[rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 3)),            # 3 real signals
          rng.integers(0, 2, (n, 1)),          # binary, low cardinality
          rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 2)),            # 2 pure noise
          np.arange(n) / n]                    # a unique ID: NO signal
names = ["signal_1", "signal_2", "signal_3", "binary", "noise_1", "noise_2", "row_id"]
y = (1.8*X[:, 0] + 1.2*X[:, 1] - .9*X[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. IMPURITY-BASED IMPORTANCE -- one tree vs a forest
# =====================================================================
dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"{'feature':>10s} {'one tree':>10s} {'forest':>9s}")
for i in np.argsort(-rf.feature_importances_):
    print(f"{names[i]:>10s} {dt.feature_importances_[i]:10.4f} "
          f"{rf.feature_importances_[i]:9.4f}")
print(f"\nboth sum to 1: {dt.feature_importances_.sum():.4f}, "
      f"{rf.feature_importances_.sum():.4f}")
# The forest averages over 300 trees, so its ranking is far more stable --
# "how important is one feature to one or more trees, not just one tree".

# STABILITY, measured:
def spread(make, k=8):
    imps = [make(s).fit(X_tr, y_tr).feature_importances_ for s in range(k)]
    return np.std(imps, axis=0).mean()
print(f"\nimportance std across seeds:")
print(f"  single tree : {spread(lambda s: DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=s)):.4f}")
print(f"  forest (300): {spread(lambda s: RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=s, n_jobs=-1)):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. COMPUTING IT BY HAND -- weighted impurity decrease
# =====================================================================
def manual_importance(tree, n_features):
    t = tree.tree_
    imp = np.zeros(n_features)
    total = t.weighted_n_node_samples[0]
    for node in range(t.node_count):
        if t.children_left[node] == -1:                # a leaf
            continue
        L, R = t.children_left[node], t.children_right[node]
        nt, nL, nR = (t.weighted_n_node_samples[node],
                      t.weighted_n_node_samples[L], t.weighted_n_node_samples[R])
        gain = t.impurity[node] - (nL/nt)*t.impurity[L] - (nR/nt)*t.impurity[R]
        imp[t.feature[node]] += (nt/total) * gain      # weight by data passing through
    return imp / imp.sum()

manual = manual_importance(dt, X.shape[1])
print(f"\nmanual == sklearn: {np.allclose(manual, dt.feature_importances_)}")
# The formula IS "the feature that reduces the impurity most is the most important",
# weighted by how much data reaches each node.

# =====================================================================
# 3. TRAP 1 -- THE CARDINALITY BIAS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\nrow_id has ZERO predictive value but gets importance "
      f"{rf.feature_importances_[6]:.4f}")
print(f"binary (also useless) gets only {rf.feature_importances_[3]:.4f}")
print(f"distinct values: row_id {len(np.unique(X[:,6]))}, binary {len(np.unique(X[:,3]))}")
# High cardinality -> more candidate splits -> more chances to reduce
# TRAINING impurity by luck. Exactly the Topic 55 bias.

# =====================================================================
# 4. PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE -- measured on HELD-OUT data
# =====================================================================
perm = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=20,
                              random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)
print(f"\n{'feature':>10s} {'impurity':>10s} {'permutation':>13s} {'+/-':>8s}")
for i in np.argsort(-perm.importances_mean):
    print(f"{names[i]:>10s} {rf.feature_importances_[i]:10.4f} "
          f"{perm.importances_mean[i]:13.4f} {perm.importances_std[i]:8.4f}")
# row_id and the noise columns now score ~0.000 -- shuffling them changes
# nothing, because the model gains nothing from them on unseen data.

# BY HAND, to show there is no magic:
base = rf.score(X_te, y_te)
print(f"\nbaseline held-out accuracy: {base:.4f}")
for j in [0, 6]:
    Xp = X_te.copy()
    drops = []
    for r in range(20):
        Xp[:, j] = np.random.default_rng(r).permutation(X_te[:, j])
        drops.append(base - rf.score(Xp, y_te))
    print(f"  shuffling {names[j]:>8s}: accuracy drops {np.mean(drops):+.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. TRAP 2 -- CORRELATED FEATURES SPLIT THE CREDIT
# =====================================================================
Xc = np.c_[X, X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, .05, n)]          # near-duplicate of signal_1
namesc = names + ["signal_1_copy"]
Xc_tr, Xc_te, _, _ = train_test_split(Xc, y, test_size=.3,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)
rfc = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xc_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\nsignal_1 importance alone          : {rf.feature_importances_[0]:.4f}")
print(f"signal_1 importance with a duplicate: {rfc.feature_importances_[0]:.4f}")
print(f"the duplicate's importance          : {rfc.feature_importances_[-1]:.4f}")
print(f"their sum                           : "
      f"{rfc.feature_importances_[0] + rfc.feature_importances_[-1]:.4f}")
# The credit is SPLIT. A threshold rule could drop BOTH.

permc = permutation_importance(rfc, Xc_te, y_te, n_repeats=15,
                               random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)
print(f"\npermutation importance also suffers:")
print(f"  signal_1  {permc.importances_mean[0]:.4f}")
print(f"  its copy  {permc.importances_mean[-1]:.4f}")
# Shuffling one leaves the model able to use the other, so BOTH look useless.
# No importance measure resolves this -- the question has no answer.

# =====================================================================
# 6. FEATURE SELECTION -- and validating it
# =====================================================================
order = np.argsort(-rf.feature_importances_)
print(f"\n{'k features kept':>16s} {'features':>34s} {'cv accuracy':>13s}")
for k in range(1, 8):
    cols = order[:k]
    s = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0,
                                               n_jobs=-1),
                        X_tr[:, cols], y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"{k:16d} {str([names[i] for i in cols]):>34s} {s:13.4f}")
# The curve plateaus once the three real signals are in. Everything after
# that is removable -- but VALIDATE, do not guess a threshold.

sfm = SelectFromModel(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0,
                                             n_jobs=-1),
                      threshold="median").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nSelectFromModel(threshold='median') keeps: "
      f"{[names[i] for i in np.flatnonzero(sfm.get_support())]}")

rfe = RFECV(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
            cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"RFECV chose {rfe.n_features_} features: "
      f"{[names[i] for i in np.flatnonzero(rfe.support_)]}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. SELECT INSIDE THE CV LOOP, NOT OUTSIDE IT
# =====================================================================
Xn = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 3000))                   # PURE NOISE
yn = rng.integers(0, 2, 200)

sel = SelectFromModel(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0,
                                             n_jobs=-1),
                      max_features=20).fit(Xn, yn)   # used ALL the labels
print(f"\nselection OUTSIDE cv, on pure noise: "
      f"{cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0), sel.transform(Xn), yn, cv=5).mean():.3f}")
print(f"selection INSIDE a pipeline        : "
      f"{cross_val_score(Pipeline([('s', SelectFromModel(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0), max_features=20)), ('m', RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0))]), Xn, yn, cv=5).mean():.3f}")
# The first number is an artefact of leakage. The second is ~0.50, correctly.

# =====================================================================
# 8. SHAP -- per-prediction attribution
# =====================================================================
# pip install shap
# import shap
# explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf)          # exact for tree ensembles
# sv = explainer.shap_values(X_te)
#
# GLOBAL importance = mean |SHAP| across rows:
#   np.abs(sv).mean(axis=0)
# LOCAL explanation for row i -- the thing impurity and permutation cannot give:
#   shap.force_plot(explainer.expected_value, sv[i], X_te[i])
#
# Additivity: for every row, sum(shap values) + base value == the prediction.
# That per-row property is why SHAP is the standard for answering
# "why was THIS application declined?" in regulated settings (Topic 06).
Worked Examples
Two importance methods on the same model
Model: a forest that predicts placement using features $A$ (CGPA) and $B$ (number of projects). Baseline accuracy on a validation set: $0.90$.
Method 1 – impurity-based (from the trees). Sum the weighted impurity decreases over all splits that use each feature, then normalise to 1:
\text{raw}_A = 0.30, \qquad \text{raw}_B = 0.10
\text{importance}_A = \frac{0.30}{0.40} = 0.75, \qquad \text{importance}_B = \frac{0.10}{0.40} = 0.25
Method 2 – permutation importance (on held-out data). Shuffle one column, keep the model fixed, and measure the accuracy drop:

Agreement and caveat. Both methods rank $A$ above $B$. Impurity importance is computed on training splits and favours high-cardinality or continuous features; permutation importance measures what the model actually relies on for prediction. When they disagree strongly, trust permutation on held-out data.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Feature importance calculates the importance of every feature,
 telling us how much each contributes to the prediction of the
 target. It is a feature selection technique — keep the
 important features, remove the unnecessary ones.

Impurity $=$ how mixed or confused the data is in a node. All
 same class $\Rightarrow$ impurity $=0$; different classes mixed
 $\Rightarrow$ impurity $>0$.

Decision Tree: the feature that reduces the impurity
 most is the most important, weighted by how much data reaches each node.

Random Forest: how important a feature is to one or more
 trees, not just one — how much overall impurity it reduces,
 averaged over all trees. Far more stable than a single tree's.

SHAP: measures the exact contribution of each feature —
 if I remove one feature, how much the prediction changes. Uniquely, it is
 computed per prediction.

Trap 1 — cardinality bias: impurity importance is computed on
 training data, so high-cardinality features (a unique ID) score highly
 with no predictive value.

Trap 2 — correlated features split the credit, so neither looks
 important alone.

Permutation importance fixes the cardinality bias: shuffle a
 column on held-out data and measure the score drop. Model-agnostic.

When selecting, validate the choice by cross-validation, and do
 the selection inside the CV loop.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How does a random forest compute feature importance?

For each node that splits on a feature, take the impurity decrease weighted by
the fraction of data reaching that node; sum over all such nodes, then average
across trees and normalise. Averaging over hundreds of trees is what makes it far
more stable than a single tree's greedy, arbitrary choices.
Q. A unique ID column shows high importance. What is going on?

The cardinality bias. Impurity importance is computed on the training data, and a
feature with thousands of distinct values can always find a split that separates
training rows slightly further by chance. Use permutation importance, which is
measured on held-out data, and the ID's score collapses to zero.
Q. What is permutation importance?

Score the fitted model on held-out data, shuffle one column to destroy its
relationship with the target, re-score, and take the drop. Model-agnostic, honest
because it uses unseen data, and immune to the cardinality bias — at the cost of
one scoring pass per feature per repeat.

Q. Two correlated features both show low importance. Should you drop
both?

No. Each tree picks one arbitrarily, so the credit is divided; and permutation
importance is worse here, since shuffling one leaves the model able to use the
other. Cluster correlated features and evaluate them as a group, or drop one and
re-measure.
Q. What does SHAP add over the other two?

Per-prediction attribution. Impurity and permutation give a single global ranking;
SHAP explains each individual prediction, with the guarantee that the
contributions plus a base value sum exactly to the output. That is what regulated
settings require when an applicant must be told why they were declined.
Q. How would you use importance for feature selection?

Rank the features, then add them one at a time and cross-validate, taking the
smallest set whose score matches the best. Do the selection inside the CV
loop — selecting on the full dataset and then cross-validating produces
excellent scores on pure noise.
